requirements.requirement: On node1, cron scheduling is restricted to root and opsadmin only.
requirements.summary: The authoritative /etc/cron.allow file contains exactly root and opsadmin, with root ownership and mode 0644. The unlisted antrieb account is explicitly denied, while root reaches the authorized “no crontab” result. After restart, the exact policy remains present and cron is active and enabled.

overall_summary: The requested cron access-control policy is correctly installed and persisted across the mandatory node restart. Restart and service recovery evidence is coherent and independently corroborated. Operational hygiene is strong apart from four small abandoned verification files in /tmp.
limitations: No direct crontab behavior test was captured for opsadmin. Initial account lookup returned only root, so the evidence does not establish that an opsadmin account currently exists; it does directly establish that the cron allowlist authorizes that username.
The fixed lifecycle snapshots do not inspect /etc/cron.allow, so policy-state verification relies on executor command output.
Four final-verification temporary files remained under /tmp after execution.

operational_hygiene.summary: All managed-system mutations had a clear task or mandatory restart-evidence purpose. The only hygiene defect is four retained temporary output files created during final verification—/tmp/antrieb-cron-post.err, /tmp/antrieb-cron-post.out, /tmp/root-cron-post.err, and /tmp/root-cron-post.out—which were not cleaned up. No failed services, package damage, or new listening sockets were observed. The restart protocol is complete and independently corroborated: healthy pre-restart state and boot ID, acknowledgement, transient SSH unavailability, a different post-restart boot ID, and recovered cron service and policy.
